lessons.notes_html:
Unit 14 teaches direct and indirect speech — the book's full narration rules — and writing for fluency, creativity and accuracy.

Direct and Indirect Speech

Direct speech reports the speaker's exact words: Maya said, "I am busy now." Indirect (reported) speech reports the message in our own words: Maya said that she was busy then. In indirect speech, tenses usually move one step back:

Direct SpeechIndirect Speech
Simple Present — "I play football."Simple Past — He said that he played football.
Present Continuous — "I am reading a novel."Past Continuous — She said that she was reading a novel.
Present Perfect — "We have finished our work."Past Perfect — They said that they had finished their work.
Simple Past — "I saw the movie."Past Perfect — He said that he had seen the movie.
Past Continuous — "I was cooking dinner."Past Perfect Continuous — She said that she had been cooking dinner.
Future — "I will call you tomorrow."Would — He said that he would call me the next day.
Future Perfect — "I will have completed my homework."Would have — She said that she would have completed her homework.

Modals, Pronouns and Time Words

  • Modals shift: can → could, may → might, shall → should, will → would, must → had to.
  • Pronouns change to fit the narrator: "I am happy" → She said that she was happy.
  • Time and place words shift: today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the day before; last week → the previous week; next year → the following year; ago → before; now → then; this → that; here → there.
  • That introduces reported statements and may often be left out (He said he would come); it is not used before questions or commands.

Questions, Orders, Requests, Suggestions, Advice

TypeRuleExample
Yes/No questionasked + if/whether"Do you like music?" → He asked if I liked music.
Wh-questionkeep the wh-word"Where are you going?" → She asked where I was going.
Order / commandordered/told + to + verb"Close the door." → He ordered me to close the door.
Negative ordertold + not to"Don't run." → She told me not to run.
Requestrequested/asked + to"Please help me." → He requested me to help him.
Suggestionsuggested + -ing"Let's go out." → He suggested going out.
Adviceadvised + to"You should study hard." → She advised me to study hard.
Universal truthNO tense changeTeacher said that the sun rises in the east.

Writing for Fluency, Creativity and Accuracy

Write freely first — multiple paragraphs of free writing for fluency, creativity and pleasure, without worrying about mistakes. Then proofread and edit: check subject–verb agreement, noun–pronoun agreement, reference words, connectives and transitional devices, punctuation and spelling. The book's model takes a rough paragraph on education ("Education are very important… it make us able…") and corrects it step by step ("Education is very important in our lives because it makes us able to understand the world…"). Clear writing is easy to understand; coherent writing flows logically; style and tone must suit the task, purpose and audience.

Key Points

  • In reported speech, tenses step back and time words shift (today → that day).
  • Universal truths never change tense.
  • Questions use if/whether or the wh-word; commands use told/ordered + to.
  • Draft freely, then proofread and edit for accuracy.

lessons.notes_html:
The Beggar and the King is a one-act play by Winthrop Parkhurst (1891–1983), an American writer appreciated for his sympathy for the oppressed; the play is reprinted from The Atlantic Book of Modern Plays (1921). Its three characters are the King of a great country, his Servant, and a Beggar.

The Annoying Voice

Midsummer. In a palace chamber the King sits in a golden chair, crown on his head, golden sceptre in hand, while his Servant fans him with an enormous fan of peacock feathers. From the street comes a voice: "Bread. Bread. Bread. Give me some bread." The King, speaking languidly (lazily), is annoyed and orders the beggar sent away. But every punishment has already been tried — "even yesterday": the beggar has been driven away many times and returns crying louder; the lash has been used; the guards have bloodied their swords; his tongue was cut out — and he grew another; he was slain — and is alive again, crying for bread. "Hunger is as food to the lungs, O king," says the Servant.

The Remedy Refused

The Servant keeps hinting at the only remedy: a crust of bread dropped from the window. The King refuses absolutely: "To feed a beggar is always foolish. Every crumb that is given to a beggar is an evil seed from which springs another fellow like him." If he gave a crust today, the beggar would be hungry again tomorrow. At last the King has his own idea: he will order the beggar to stop himself.

The Beggar in the Royal Chamber

The beggar — a shambling creature in filthy rags — is brought in. The King commands: "Do not beg any more." The beggar answers faintly, again and again: "I — I do not understand." He is not deaf: "The words of thy mouth I can hear perfectly. But their noise is only a foolish tinkling in my ears." He refuses to touch his forehead to the floor: "I have made no promise. Neither have I any king." Then he turns the tables and commands the King: remove your crown and throw it from the window into the street — "for when thou hast thrown thy crown into the street, then will I no longer be obliged to beg." The King cries insolence and treason, but the beggar is unmoved: the soldiers' spears are as straws against his body; he is stronger than a mountain, stronger than the sea. One day, he warns, he will return with a mouth filled with rushing wind and arms like steel rods, blow over the palace, and beat upon a drum with the King's head for a drumstick: "Remember, O king, and be afraid!"

The Ending

The beggar walks out; the Servant, struck dumb, cannot move or call the guards. Outside, the voice rises again: "Bread. Bread. Give me some bread." The King, half-frightened, almost instinctively raises his hands to his crown and seems about to toss it from the window — but with an oath he presses it firmly back on his head: "How! Am I afraid of a beggar!" He shouts, "Close that window!" — as the beggar's voice grows louder and the curtain falls.

Theme

The central theme is human equality and the true value of kindness and humility. True greatness does not stem from power, wealth or position, but from compassion, understanding and respect for others; appearances and social status can be deceptive, and every human being deserves dignity and empathy. The book also states it plainly: pride leads to the downfall of man. The King represents power; the beggar symbolizes humility and poverty; the play teaches respect for humanity and promotes compassion. The beggar is the voice of truth and justice that cannot be silenced — not by the lash, not by the sword, not even by death.

Key Points

  • The beggar cannot be silenced: driven away, lashed, tongue cut out, even slain — he returns.
  • The Servant's remedy — one crust of bread — is refused by the King again and again.
  • Face to face, the beggar demands the crown be thrown from the window; the King refuses.
  • The King is left afraid, pressing his crown on his head while the voice grows louder.

lessons.notes_html:
The book's Glossary explains the key words of the play.

Words and Meanings

WordMeaning
sceptreA decorated staff held by a king or queen as a symbol of authority.
enormousExtremely large — the servant's enormous fan of peacock feathers.
languidlyLazily, without energy — the King speaks languidly.
jestA joke; to speak in fun. "Do not jest with thy king."
riddlesPuzzling questions or statements. "I do not like riddles. They confuse my brain."
flingTo throw with force — "fling him a crust from the window."
exceedinglyVery, extremely. "This fellow is exceedingly hungry."
illustriousFamous and much admired — "O great and illustrious king."
remedyA cure or solution to a problem — a crust of bread is the remedy.
fanningWaving a fan to create a breeze.
tortureSevere pain inflicted as punishment. The beggar cannot be tortured — he feels no pain.
contaminateTo make dirty or impure. The servant fears the beggar will contaminate the King's lips.
abashedEmbarrassed or ashamed — the servant goes out abashed.
deafUnable to hear. The beggar is not deaf — he hears every word.
tinkleA light ringing sound — the King's words are "a foolish tinkling" to the beggar.
solemnlySeriously and formally — "promise solemnly."
offendTo insult or displease — "the noise of my voice offends thee."
slainKilled (past participle of slay).
bodingA feeling that something bad will happen — "thy days will be filled with a terrible boding."
insolenceRude disrespect — the King calls the beggar's words insolence.
treasonBetrayal of one's country or king — a crime punished by death.
hurricaneA violent storm — "my words are more fearful than a hurricane."
seizeTo grab or arrest suddenly — "Seize him!"
impudenceRudeness, shameless boldness.
dumbUnable to speak — the servant is struck dumb.
snapTo break suddenly — "I will snap the bones in thy body."
oathA swear word; also a solemn promise.
tossTo throw lightly — the King almost tosses his crown out.
instinctivelyWithout thinking, by natural impulse — the King instinctively reaches for his crown.

Key Points

  • A sceptre is the king's staff of authority; a remedy is a cure or solution.
  • Treason is betrayal of the king; insolence and impudence are rude disrespect.
  • Slain means killed; dumb means unable to speak.

lessons.notes_html:
Unit 15 is a drama unit: it teaches the elements and stages of a play, organizational patterns, performance skills, and play-script writing.

Elements and Stages of Plot Development

  • Exposition — introduces the characters, setting and main situation: a palace chamber in midsummer; the King on his golden chair; a beggar crying for bread outside.
  • Rising action — conflicts build: every punishment fails; the beggar is summoned into the royal chamber.
  • Climax — the turning point: the beggar commands the King to throw his crown from the window and warns him of the day of reckoning.
  • Falling action — the beggar leaves; the servant cannot move; the voice sounds again outside.
  • Resolution (denouement) — the King, afraid, presses his crown back on his head and orders the window closed, but the voice grows louder: he cannot silence the beggar, even in death. The beggar's voice symbolizes the persistence of truth and justice.

Problem, Plot, Resolution, Theme

  • Problem: the conflict between the King, who wants to silence the beggar's complaints, and the Beggar, who wants justice and fairness.
  • Plot: the beggar proves the King has power only while his servants allow it; by defying him, the beggar promises to haunt the King and humble him.
  • Resolution: the King realizes he cannot silence the beggar's voice.
  • Theme: pride leads to the downfall of man; gold cannot give power — only facing difficulties and learning can.

Organizational Patterns

Texts are organized by patterns such as list/sequence of ideas, comparison–contrast, cause–effect, problem–solution, and reasons/assumptions–conclusion. This play mainly follows problem–solution: the problem (the beggar's crying annoys the King) meets attempted solutions (punishments, the refused crust, the royal command) — and the one true solution, kindness, is never tried.

Performance: Tone, Body Language, Expression

  • Tone: the way a character speaks to match the situation, emotion or personality — harsh for the King's rage, gentle or faint for the beggar's calm.
  • Body language: movements and gestures that express feelings — crossing arms for anger, slouching for sadness, clapping for excitement.
  • Dramatic expression: voice, gestures, facial expressions and emotions together bring a character to life — fear shown by trembling, a shaky voice and widened eyes.
  • Choose dialogues deliberately so the contrasting social positions — and the play's message of dignity and equality — come out clearly.

Writing a Short Play Script

A play script gives character names before their speeches, stage directions in brackets (entrances, actions, feelings), and dialogue that carries the story. Write with correct mechanics — grammar, punctuation, spelling and paragraphing — and let the interaction itself highlight the theme, as the King–Beggar exchange highlights human dignity and equality.

Key Points

  • Every play moves through exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution.
  • This play's pattern is problem–solution; the untried solution is kindness.
  • Performance = tone + body language + dramatic expression.
  • In a script, stage directions go in brackets and names precede speeches.
